The only file I read outside my own directory was the production estimator, sycophancy_phase0/src/sycophancy_phase0/analysis/g6_iv.py.

(1) Theorem 1 is correct as stated. P(R|D)−P(R'|D) = E[δ1_D]/π. E[δ] = 0 because, given r and under A0, (t, K32+K96, η) has the same law as (t, K'128, η). Cauchy–Schwarz then gives |Cov(δ,1_D)| ≤ σ_δ·sqrt(π(1−π)). The selection term follows the same way. The theorem is an elementary bound, and its substance is the constants.

(2) Exact arithmetic, using rational Beta moments, the joint falling-factorial moment identity, and the Vandermonde form of Ũ_j, reproduces the claimed values exactly:
- U_1 pilot share = 1/4 exactly.
- U_2 share (narrow) = 221679769/894945124 = 0.247702, bit-identical. Half-variance gives 0.24762.
- Ũ_2(5, 0.2) = 0.0354823.
- κ (narrow lin/quad/cheb) = 0.0934/0.0826/0.2299; half-variance = 0.0868/0.0772/0.2093.
- ME share of the type-direction variance = 0.0450 (narrow lin) / 0.2786 (narrow cheb).
- The orderings Φ ⪯ Σ^ME ⪯ Σ hold: the minimum eigenvalues of both difference matrices are positive.
The wide-world Beta parameters are not given in the assumptions, so the wide κ cannot be checked. A guessed Beta(5,20)/(6.25,18.75) gives 0.0979/0.0862/0.2428, close to the claimed values.

(3) Nested Monte Carlo. My vectorized copy of endpoint_contrast_poly_cs(degree=2) matches the production function to 1e-13 on t-values for both HC1 and CR1, and agrees on the PD flag. With 8000 outer pilots × 200 inner draws (8 times the author's run), the point σ_δ and 95% UCL for REJECT are:

| cell | HC1 point / UCL (claimed UCL) | CR1 point / UCL (claimed UCL) |
|---|---|---|
| narrow lin | ≈0 / 0.0020 (0.0064) | ≈0 / 0.0015 (0.0051) |
| narrow quad | ≈0 / 0.0026 (0.0041) | 0.0012 / 0.0031 (0.0038) |
| narrow cheb | 0.0059 / 0.0066 (0.0085) | 0.0064 / 0.0072 (0.0075) |
| half-variance lin | 0.0034 / 0.0041 (0.0047) | 0.0041 / 0.0048 (0.0061) |

All of the author's UCLs are conservative relative to these more precise estimates. The other quoted constants:
- NON-PD (half-variance): point 0.0359, 90% CI [0.0351, 0.0368], against the claimed UCL of 0.0357. That claimed "upper limit" sits slightly below my point estimate, so it is not quite an upper limit, though the difference is small.
- WIDTH ≤ 0.15: half-variance 0.0810 (claimed 0.0849); narrow lin 0.0316 (claimed 0.0322).
- σ_0: my UCLs are 0.0020/0.0014/0.0033/0.0004, all within the claimed values.
- One-stage size, narrow lin: 0.0451 reuse vs 0.0448 fresh (claimed 0.0450 vs 0.0456).
- One-stage size, half-variance: 0.0215 reuse vs 0.0217 fresh, ±0.0001. The claimed reuse value of 0.0223 is about 2.3 of its own SEs high, which is chance, since E[δ] = 0 exactly.

(4) Attack with concrete rules. I tried rules that use only (t, K32), each taken as an upper or lower tail at π = 0.5 and 0.1: the type gap in r̂, the within-type variance of r̂, the degree-2 PD margin at m = 32, skewness, the maximum, and the count of zeros. None exceeded the bound. The largest REJECT reuse effects were:
- half-variance lin, high within-type variance at π = 0.1: +0.0075 ± 0.0009, against a bound of 0.0141;
- narrow cheb CR1, same rule: +0.0059, against 0.0225;
- narrow lin: at most 0.0039 at π = 0.1 (bound 0.019), and 0.0019 at π = 0.5 (bound 0.0064).
The same rules move NON-PD by up to ±0.047 and WIDTH by up to ±0.14 in the half-variance world. This matches the disclosed caveat that those events are not small.

Overstatements found, none of which breaks the bound:
(a) Prop. 2 calls φ_i = E[ψ_i | r_i, K32_i] the "pilot-tiltable part". But φ_i depends on the unobserved r_i. The part a (t, K32)-measurable rule can actually tilt is E[φ_i | t_i, K32_i]. Recomputed exactly, κ along the type direction is 0.0826/0.0722/0.2022 (narrow) and 0.0808/0.0711/0.1939 (half-variance), roughly 7–13% below the quoted values. Calling κ the "maximal" tilt is therefore wrong: κ is only an upper bound. The Cauchy–Schwarz cap is also attained only for a two-point score; for an approximately Gaussian sum at π = 1/2 the maximum is about 0.80 of the cap.
(b) "The sup is attained by {δ > q_{1−π}}" needs randomization at atoms. δ is a function of a discrete vector, so an exact P(D) = π may not be reachable without it.
(c) The "≤ 0.0085 for ANY rule" statement is a per-cell 95% Monte Carlo bound for four (world, g) cells, not a proved one. The scope does say this.
